title: We Think We Understand, But Do We?
author: Lee LeFever
summary: Lee LeFever continues his series on understanding by arguing that familiarity is easily mistaken for comprehension. He reviews Rebecca Lawson's 2006 bicycle experiments, in which many non-experts rated their knowledge highly and then made drawing errors when asked to sketch the pedals, chain and frame. He pairs this with Rozenblit and Keil's 2002 study of the illusion of explanatory depth, in which students lowered their self-ratings after trying to explain a speedometer, a toilet or a watch. The mechanism, he says, is not a character flaw: understanding costs attention and working memory, so minds settle for a feeling of fit. The practical advice is for communicators and teachers to check their own understanding by writing out mechanisms and to make causal chains visible rather than trusting nodding heads. The post closes by previewing how the mind organizes knowledge into patterns that can also mislead.
points: The illusion of explanatory depth means people rate their understanding highly until they must explain a mechanism, which is when the gaps appear.
In Lawson's bicycle study, 44 and 60 percent of the two non-expert groups made at least one drawing error, against 9 percent of experts, despite confident self-ratings.
Understanding is effortful, so minds default to quick resolution, which is a natural process rather than a lack of intelligence.
Explaining is itself a diagnostic: asking learners to write out how something works forces them to reckon with what they actually know.
For teachers and communicators, visible nodding is weak evidence of understanding, so explanations should build context and show the causal chain.
quotes: Understanding is often hard work. It uses up attention, working memory, and other mental resources. We don’t always invest the effort needed to examine how something works.

This isn’t a character flaw or lack of intelligence but a natural way the mind processes information. Our minds seek resolution or fit, and often, we convince ourselves that a subject is resolved without a full understanding.
44% and 60% of the two non-expert groups made at least one drawing error, compared with 9% of experts.

They do not appear to understand a simple set of causal relations (turning the pedals turns the chain that spins the back wheel that drives the bicycle forward); therefore, they do not know how turning the pedals moves a bicycle.

Consistently, the students lowered their level of understanding of the device after attempting to explain it. This led the researchers to conclude that having to explain concepts and mechanisms forces people to reckon with what they understand, or not.
The people confidently nodding their heads may feel as if they understand, but it could easily be an illusion. Build context. Make the connections visible. Show the causal chain.
One way of testing for understanding is to test if the person would know what would have happened if something was different.
